questions.question: Describe the Timbuktu manuscripts and explain why they are important historical sources.
questions.expected_answer: Hundreds of thousands of handwritten documents, mostly in Arabic and some in Ajami, mainly from the 1500s to early 1900s, covering religion, law, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, history, geography and poetry, plus letters and trade records; mostly held by families. They show West Africans recording their own history and knowledge from an African perspective and disprove claims that Africa had no written history.

questions.question: Explain South Africa's role in the Timbuktu Manuscripts Project.
questions.expected_answer: After President Thabo Mbeki's visit in 2001, South Africa launched the South Africa-Mali Project, NEPAD's first official cultural project, raising funds through a trust to build a new Ahmed Baba Institute building (handed over in 2009) and training Malian conservators at the National Archives in Pretoria; UCT researchers studied the manuscripts. It showed African co-operation in protecting African heritage.

questions.question: What is a World Heritage Site, why was Timbuktu listed, and what happened to its heritage in 2012-2013?
questions.expected_answer: A place UNESCO recognises as having outstanding universal value to all humanity. Timbuktu was listed in 1988 for its Djinguereber, Sankore and Sidi Yahya mosques and its cemeteries and mausoleums, representing its golden age of learning and trade and the spread of Islam. In 2012 armed groups occupied the city, destroyed mausoleums and in 2013 burned about 4 000 manuscripts; most manuscripts were smuggled to Bamako; it was placed on the danger list and the mausoleums were rebuilt by 2015.
